title: 22. Interview: Layer 4 Load Balancer
summary: Interview Q&A for Layer 4 Load Balancer — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Layer 4 Load Balancer interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What information does a Layer 4 load balancer use to make routing decisions, and what does it deliberately ignore?
**Answer:** A Layer 4 balancer uses only the OSI transport-layer header: source IP, source port, destination IP (the VIP), destination port, and protocol number (TCP or UDP) — collectively the "5-tuple." It deliberately ignores everything above layer 4: the HTTP method, URL path, headers, cookies, TLS SNI, request body, and response codes are all invisible. The decision is made per-connection (for TCP) or per-flow (for UDP via a hash + timeout) at the moment the SYN arrives, and once chosen, every subsequent packet on that connection goes to the same backend. This is what makes L4 fast — there is no parsing, no buffering, no per-request logic — and what makes it protocol-agnostic: it works identically for HTTP, gRPC, MQTT, PostgreSQL wire protocol, Kafka's binary protocol, and any TCP/UDP service. The trade-off is that content-aware routing (`/api/*` to service A, `/static/*` to service B) is impossible without L7, and TLS cannot be terminated (only passed through).
**Visual:**
```
L4 sees:    {src_ip, src_port, dst_ip=VIP, dst_port, proto}
L4 ignores: method, URL, headers, cookies, body, TLS SNI
            -> routes per-connection, sticky for life of flow
```

### Q2. Explain NAT mode vs. Direct Server Return (DSR) and when you would choose each.
**Answer:** In **NAT mode**, the balancer rewrites both directions of the connection: client→backend packets have their destination IP changed from VIP to backend IP, and backend→client replies have their source IP changed back to VIP. Both directions traverse the balancer, so the balancer's bandwidth must handle the sum of request and response traffic. In **DSR mode**, the balancer rewrites only the destination MAC (not IP) on the request and forwards to the backend; the backend has the VIP configured as a loopback alias and replies directly to the client, bypassing the balancer entirely. DSR is chosen when response bandwidth dwarfs request bandwidth — video streaming (Netflix), large-file downloads, log shipping — because the balancer's egress capacity is freed. NAT is chosen when the response fits in the balancer's pipe, when backends cannot be configured with the VIP loopback trick (e.g., managed cloud DBs), or when you need the balancer to see both directions for logging or access control. AWS NLB uses NAT-like behavior; classic HAProxy and LVS support both modes; CDNs almost universally use DSR for video.
**Visual:**
```
NAT:    client <-> LB <-> backend     (both ways through LB)
DSR:    client -> LB -> backend       (request)
        client  <-  backend           (response skips LB)
        used for: video, large files, downloads
```

### Q3. Why is L4 called "protocol-agnostic," and what are some real-world protocols it load-balances that L7 cannot?
**Answer:** L4 is protocol-agnostic because it never parses the application payload — it only deals with TCP/UDP ports and IP addresses. Therefore any protocol that runs over TCP or UDP can be load-balanced identically: the balancer does not care whether the bytes are HTTP, gRPC, MQTT, SMTP, or a custom binary protocol. Real-world examples that L7 cannot handle: **PostgreSQL wire protocol** (a stateful binary connection that authenticates once and multiplexes queries — there is no HTTP equivalent); **Kafka's binary protocol** (clients need direct TCP to a specific broker for partition leadership, and the protocol has no HTTP surface); **Cassandra's native transport** (Netflix load-balances Cassandra clusters behind L4); **Redis RESP** (L4 HAProxy is the standard Redis Cluster front-end); **MQTT** for IoT (long-lived stateful TCP); **SSH, RDP, VNC** (no HTTP layer at all); **DNS over UDP** (a stateless UDP protocol, no HTTP parsing possible). The same AWS NLB can front an HTTPS web tier and a Kafka pool — that generality is the value.
**Visual:**
```
L4 can balance:  HTTP, HTTPS(passthrough), gRPC, MQTT, SMTP,
                 PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, Kafka, Cassandra,
                 DNS/UDP, SSH, RDP, gaming UDP, custom binary
L7 can balance:  HTTP, HTTPS(terminated), gRPC, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
                 (anything with parseable L7 headers)
```

### Q4. What state does an L4 load balancer hold, and what happens to active connections if the balancer crashes?
**Answer:** An L4 balancer in NAT mode holds a per-flow connection table — one entry per active TCP/UDP flow, keyed by the 5-tuple, mapping to the chosen backend and holding sequence-number offsets for NAT. Thousands to millions of entries are typical; this is why L4 balancers need generous memory for high-connection-count workloads. If the balancer crashes, **every active connection is dropped** — the new active balancer (after VRRP/keepalived failover) has no record of those flows, and even if it did, the backends are mid-stream with sequence numbers expecting the old balancer. The mitigation is **connection table sync** between the active and standby: keepalived's `lvs_sync_daemon` and Conntrackd replicate the connection table to the standby so it can pick up existing flows on failover (with some boundary-packet drops). UDP is more forgiving — flows are hashed, not stateful — but a failover still causes brief misrouting. DSR mode is more resilient: because backends talk directly to clients, a balancer crash only affects new connections, not existing ones. This is one of the strongest arguments for DSR in long-lived connection workloads.
**Visual:**
```
NAT balancer crash:
  conn table gone -> ALL active TCP flows dropped
  fix: keepalived sync daemon replicates table to standby
       (still some loss at failover boundary)

DSR balancer crash:
  existing connections unaffected (backends reply directly)
  only NEW connections during failover window are lost
```

### Q5. Why can't an L4 load balancer terminate TLS, and what does "TLS pass-through" mean?
**Answer:** TLS termination requires parsing the TLS handshake — specifically, reading the ClientHello's SNI (Server Name Indication) field to know which certificate to present, then performing the cryptographic exchange to decrypt subsequent application data. That requires reading layer 7 bytes inside the TCP stream, which an L4 balancer by definition does not do. "TLS pass-through" means the balancer forwards the encrypted TCP stream byte-for-byte to a backend, which performs the TLS handshake itself — the balancer never sees the plaintext or the certificate. The trade-off: pass-through preserves end-to-end encryption (good for compliance) and is faster (no crypto on the balancer), but the balancer cannot inspect SNI to route by hostname, cannot inject headers like `X-Forwarded-For`, and cannot manage certificates centrally — each backend must hold the cert. Modern L4+ balancers (AWS NLB with TLS listener, HAProxy with SNI passthrough) can do a limited form of SNI inspection without full termination: they peek at the ClientHello's SNI to route to the right backend pool, then pass the encrypted stream through. This is a hybrid that retains encryption while gaining host-based routing, at the cost of more complex implementation.
**Visual:**
```
L4 pass-through:    client ===TLS=== LB ===TLS=== backend
                    (LB sees ciphertext only, no SNI routing)

L4+ SNI peek:       client ==TLS==> LB peeks at ClientHello SNI
                                LB routes by hostname, passes TLS through
                                (still no decryption, no header injection)

L7 termination:     client ==TLS==> LB decrypts, reads HTTP
                                LB re-encrypts to backend (or plaintext)
                                (full content access, but LB is a crypto bottleneck)
```

### Q6. What is Google Maglev, and why is it significant in the history of L4 load balancing?
**Answer:** Maglev is Google's in-house software L4 load balancer, documented in a 2016 NSDI paper, that fronts the ingress traffic for every Google service (Search, YouTube, Gmail, etc.) on commodity Linux servers. It is significant for three reasons. First, it proved that **software L4 can match bespoke hardware** — each Maglev node sustains tens of millions of packets per second, enough to handle Google's scale without F5-style ASICs. Second, it introduced **consistent hashing for packet-level distribution** — instead of per-flow state tables that grow with connection count, Maglev precomputes a lookup table mapping each 5-tuple hash to a backend, so lookup is O(1) memory access with no per-flow state. When a backend is added or removed, only ~1/N of flows are remapped, minimizing disruption. Third, it democratized the architecture — the design influenced AWS NLB, Cloudflare's Magic Transit, and the broader shift to software-defined load balancing. The key insight: with a big enough consistent-hash table (Maglev uses 65,537 entries per VIP), you can have stateless L4 routing that survives node failure cleanly and scales horizontally by adding Maglev nodes behind an ECMP Anycast VIP.
**Visual:**
```
ECMP Anycast VIP: 1.2.3.4 announced by N Maglev nodes
                  switch hashes 5-tuple -> one Maglev node
                  Maglev node: lookup table[ hash(5-tuple) ] -> backend
                  -> stateless, consistent, ~1/N disruption on backend change
```

### Q7. When should you choose L4 over L7, and when must you use L7?
**Answer:** Choose L4 when: (1) you need raw throughput measured in millions of connections/sec or tens of Gbps; (2) the protocol is not HTTP — database, message broker, MQTT, gaming UDP, SSH; (3) connections are long-lived and stateful — WebSocket, gRPC streaming, database connections; (4) you want to preserve end-to-end TLS without a decryption surface; (5) you need the balancer to be a thin, low-latency, low-CPU layer. Use L7 when: (1) you need content-based routing (`/api/*` vs `/static/*`); (2) you need TLS termination to offload crypto from backends; (3) you need header rewriting, cookie injection, or request/response transformation; (4) you need per-request observability (HTTP status, latency by path); (5) you need protocol-level features like gRPC method routing or HTTP/2 multiplexing. Most production sites use **both** in a two-tier architecture: L4 (NLB) at the front for connection throughput, L7 (ALB, NGINX, Envoy) behind it for HTTP logic. Netflix and Uber both run this pattern: NLB → Zuul/NGINX → backend fleet.
**Visual:**
```
L4 (NLB, HAProxy-TCP, Maglev):
  millions of conns/sec, protocol-agnostic, no HTTP awareness
  use for: Kafka, Redis, Postgres, MQTT, raw TCP, video DSR

L7 (ALB, NGINX, Envoy):
  HTTP parsing, content routing, TLS termination
  use for: web APIs, gRPC method routing, header rewriting

Two-tier: NLB (L4) -> ALB/NGINX fleet (L7) -> backend services
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are deploying a Kafka cluster on AWS. Should you use an ALB, NLB, or no load balancer at all in front of the brokers?
**Answer:** Use an **NLB** (or no balancer, with brokers directly addressable) — never an ALB. Kafka clients need direct TCP connections to specific brokers because partition leadership is per-broker: a producer sending to partition `topic-foo-3` must talk to whichever broker is currently the leader for that partition, and the Kafka protocol handles its own routing via metadata requests. An ALB is wrong because it parses HTTP, and Kafka's binary protocol is not HTTP — the ALB would reject the connection. An NLB is correct because it is L4 (TCP passthrough), handles millions of connections, and integrates cleanly with MSK (Amazon Managed Streaming for Kafka). Many Kafka deployments skip the balancer entirely and put brokers behind Route 53 round-robin DNS, because the client's metadata API already knows the broker endpoints — the balancer adds a hop without value. The exception is when brokers run in private subnets and clients are outside AWS: then NLB is the right ingress, providing a stable VIP that fans out to broker nodes.
**Visual:**
```
Kafka client -> metadata API -> broker endpoints (direct TCP)
                            OR
Kafka client -> NLB (TCP passthrough) -> broker pool
ALB? NO -- Kafka is not HTTP, ALB rejects the binary protocol
```

### Q2. Your video streaming service is bandwidth-limited at the load balancer. How do you scale beyond the balancer's egress capacity?
**Answer:** Switch to **Direct Server Return (DSR)** — the canonical fix for response-bandwidth-bound services. In NAT mode, the balancer must carry both the request (small HTTP range request, ~1 KB) and the response (a 2 GB video segment, e.g.) — so the balancer's egress pipe is the bottleneck. In DSR mode, the balancer forwards only the request packet to the backend (rewriting only the MAC, not the IP), and the backend responds directly to the client using the VIP as its source IP (configured as a loopback alias on each backend). The balancer's egress is freed up — it only sees the small requests, not the large responses — so a single balancer can front a fleet of backends each pumping gigabits of video. Netflix's Open Connect appliances use this pattern: the balancer handles request routing, and each Open Connect box streams video directly to the client. If DSR is impossible (e.g., backends are managed cloud instances that can't configure loopback VIPs), the alternative is to scale the balancer horizontally — multiple NLB nodes behind an Anycast VIP — and shard clients across them.
**Visual:**
```
NAT mode (bottleneck):   client <- 2GB video <- LB <- backend
                                          ^^^ LB pipe saturated
DSR mode (scales):       client <- 2GB video <-  backend
                         client -> 1KB req  ->  LB -> backend
                                          ^^^ LB only sees small reqs
```

### Q3. You have a stateful WebSocket service (chat). Can you load-balance it with L7, or do you need L4?
**Answer:** Either works, but the requirements differ. **L7 with sticky sessions** (ALB with stickiness enabled, or NGINX with `ip_hash`) routes the initial HTTP upgrade request to a backend, then pins all subsequent packets on that connection to the same backend — ALB does this naturally because it's connection-oriented at the application layer. **L4** routes by 5-tuple, which means every packet on a given TCP connection goes to the same backend — also sticky, but at the transport layer. The catch with L7: if the L7 balancer multiplexes HTTP/2 requests across backends, a single WebSocket connection can be split — but ALB specifically does not multiplex WebSockets, it treats them as upgraded TCP. For most chat workloads, ALB is fine. The deeper issue is **scaling the connection itself** — if a single backend holds 100k WebSocket connections and dies, all 100k users must reconnect. The right architecture is consistent-hash routing on user ID (so the same user lands on the same backend), external session state in Redis (so any backend can pick up a reconnected user), and graceful backend draining (close WebSockets with a 1001 going-away code so clients reconnect cleanly to a new backend).
**Visual:**
```
L7 ALB:    client --HTTP upgrade--> ALB --sticky--> backend (chat server)
           all WS frames on this conn -> same backend (ALB doesn't multiplex WS)
L4 NLB:    client --TCP--> NLB --5-tuple hash--> backend (chat server)
           same result, lower overhead
Better: consistent-hash on user_id + Redis session state -> any backend
        can resume, surviving single-backend death
```

### Q4. Your NLB has 1 million concurrent connections and you're hitting memory limits. What's going on and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** NLB (and any NAT-mode L4 balancer) holds a per-flow entry in its connection table for every active connection — typically 200–400 bytes per flow. One million flows = ~200–400 MB of state, which sounds fine, but the kernel's `nf_conntrack` table (or the equivalent in the balancer's data plane) is often bounded by default and degrades non-linearly as it fills. Fixes, in priority order: (1) **reduce idle timeout** — NLB defaults to 350 seconds for TCP; if your workload is short-lived requests, drop to 60–90 seconds so flows expire faster; (2) **scale the balancer horizontally** — add more NLB nodes (AWS auto-scales them, but you can also front multiple NLBs with Anycast); (3) **switch to DSR** if the workload permits (long-lived flows, no NAT state on the balancer); (4) **switch to a connectionless model** — for short requests, HTTP keep-alive reduces connection count by 10–100×, or HTTP/2 multiplexing collapses many logical streams onto one TCP connection; (5) **move state off the balancer entirely** — Maglev-style consistent hashing eliminates per-flow state, looking up the backend by hash of the 5-tuple with no table. The diagnostic: monitor `nf_conntrack_count` vs `nf_conntrack_max` on the balancer's underlying nodes; if ratio > 0.7, you're approaching the cliff.
**Visual:**
```
1M flows x ~300 bytes = ~300 MB state on LB
                         ^
   fixes: shorter idle timeout (60s vs 350s)
          scale LB horizontally (more nodes)
          DSR mode (no per-flow state)
          HTTP/2 multiplexing (fewer TCP conns)
          Maglev-style stateless hashing
```

### Q5. You are load-balancing a Redis Cluster. The balancer routes by 5-tuple, but you see uneven load — some shards are hot. Why?
**Answer:** Redis Cluster sharding is by **hash slot** — 16,384 slots distributed across nodes, with `slot = CRC16(key) % 16384`. A client should talk directly to the node owning the relevant slot; if it talks to the wrong node, Redis returns a `MOVED` redirect. Putting an L4 balancer in front of Redis Cluster breaks this model: the balancer routes by 5-tuple (typically source-IP hash), which has no relationship to the Redis key. The result: a client that needs to read 100 different keys might hit 100 different balancer-selected backends, each issuing `MOVED` redirects, doubling round-trips and creating uneven load because the source-IP hash is correlated with client, not with key. The fix: **don't load-balance Redis Cluster with a generic L4 balancer**. Either use a Redis-aware client (lettuce, Jedis, redigo) that maintains a per-node connection pool and follows `MOVED` redirects, or use a Redis proxy like `envoy.filters.network.redis_proxy` or Twemproxy that understands the protocol and routes by key. For non-clustered Redis (single master + replicas), L4 works fine — HAProxy in TCP mode is the standard pattern, with replicas selected by least-connections for read scaling.
**Visual:**
```
WRONG:  client -> L4 (5-tuple hash) -> random Redis node -> MOVED redirect
                          ^- hash is unrelated to Redis key, causes churn
RIGHT:  client -> Redis-aware client/proxy (key-aware routing)
                          -> node owning the slot directly
        (or use L4 only for read-replica fan-out, not slot routing)
```

### Q6. Your L4 balancer fails over to standby, and 5% of active connections drop. The rest survive. Why didn't all of them drop?
**Answer:** You are running **connection table sync** between the active and standby balancers (keepalived's `lvs_sync_daemon` or Conntrackd), which replicates the per-flow state. Most flows survive because the standby has the table and can continue NAT'ing them. The 5% that drop fall in three categories: (1) **flows established in the last sync interval** — if sync runs every second, flows established in the last sub-second window haven't been replicated yet; (2) **flows mid-handshake** at the failover moment — the SYN-ACK was sent by the old balancer, the new one has the table entry but the sequence numbers may be off, causing the client to RST; (3) **flows with stale TCP state** — the standby's table shows ESTABLISHED but the actual TCP sequence numbers have advanced during the failover gap, and the first packet from the backend may not match the standby's NAT expectations. The fix: reduce sync interval (every 100ms instead of 1s), ensure the standby is on a low-latency link to active (sub-ms LAN), and accept that ~1–5% connection loss on failover is the practical floor — which is why long-lived connections should be designed to reconnect gracefully (exponential backoff, session resumption). For 100% survival, you need DSR mode where existing flows don't depend on the balancer at all.
**Visual:**
```
Active LB --sync every 1s--> Standby LB (has ~95% of conn table)
   |
   crash
   v
Standby takes over VIP (VRRP/ARP)
   - 95% of flows: table entry exists, NAT continues
   - 5% drop:
       * flows < 1s old (not yet synced)
       * flows mid-handshake (seq number mismatch)
       * flows with stale state (table says ESTABLISHED,
         but TCP seq has advanced during failover)
```

### Q7. You have an L4 balancer in front of an HTTPS service. Marketing wants to add hostname-based routing (api.example.com vs www.example.com to different backends). What are your options?
**Answer:** Three options, in increasing complexity. (1) **Move to L7 (ALB or NGINX/Envoy)** — terminate TLS at the L7 balancer, route by Host header. This is the standard solution, gains full HTTP features, but adds L7 overhead and a TLS termination surface. (2) **L4+ with SNI peeking** — modern L4 balancers (AWS NLB with TLS listener, HAProxy with `ssl reqsni`) can inspect the ClientHello's SNI field without terminating TLS, route to a backend pool by hostname, and pass the encrypted stream through. This preserves end-to-end encryption but requires backends to hold the certificates (no central cert management). (3) **Two-tier: L4 NLB → multiple L7 ALBs** — the NLB handles the raw TCP throughput, fans out by SNI to multiple ALBs (one per hostname), each ALB terminates TLS and routes by HTTP path. This is the AWS-recommended pattern for high-throughput multi-host HTTPS sites — NLB gives you millions of connections, ALB gives you content routing. The trade-off: option 1 is simplest but loses L4 throughput; option 2 keeps L4 speed but is operationally fiddly; option 3 is most flexible but adds architectural complexity. Most teams start with option 1 and graduate to option 3 only when throughput justifies it.
**Visual:**
```
Option 1 (L7):    client ==TLS==> ALB (terminate) -> route by Host -> backend
Option 2 (L4+):   client ==TLS==> NLB (peek SNI) -> route by hostname -> backend
                            (pass-through, backends hold certs)
Option 3 (two-tier): client ==TLS==> NLB --SNI--> ALB-api (terminate) -> api backends
                                       \--SNI--> ALB-www (terminate) -> www backends
```
